title: Heart Sutra Part 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett shares a personal experience of feeling uncertain about attending a ritual, but ultimately realizes it was because they are a Dharma teacher, highlighting the importance of self-awareness in our spiritual practice. They discuss the Heart Sutra's teachings on emptiness and dependent origination, which reveal that nothing is fixed and everything is interconnected, leading to freedom from suffering by understanding the nature of reality. This understanding encourages us to see beyond our perceptions and judgments, recognizing that they are often based on incomplete information, and instead cultivates flexibility, resilience, and liberation.

sentences.text: When I woke up this morning at five something or other, the part of me that talks to myself about what I'm doing and what I want to do didn't really get why I was coming down here.
I could have gone back to bed, but I came anyway.
When I got here I still had that feeling: what am I doing here?
You seem like nice people and a nice place, but why am I here?
Then we did a little ritual together to open the day, and I had a part in it.
I knew how to do that, although I noticed I made a few mistakes.
And we did that little ritual.
A little bit later we had a time for interviews.
I sat in a little room and several people came to see me, and we had some wonderful conversations.
Then that part of my mind that talks to myself about what's happening said, oh, you're a Dharma teacher, that's why you're here.
I really didn't know that before that moment.
So that's our topic for today.
We were looking at the Heart Sutra on Wednesday.
The Heart Sutra brings up the topic of emptiness, the teaching of emptiness from Mahayana Buddhism.
I'll talk a little more about that, and also about a connected, tightly interwoven teaching called dependent origination.
The basic idea is that nothing is fixed.
Everything is created by innumerable conditions coming together.
Any idea we have is a little bit off, a little bit behind, a little bit ahead, a little bit distorted.
Sometimes one of the benefits of practice is that we get pleasantly confused, which was my experience this morning.
If we're not holding our ideas so tightly, it's a little more possible for circumstances to show us what's happening, and who we are.
The idea is that who we are is not so fixed, and what things are is not so fixed.
Everything is flowing and changing in an interdependent, cooperative, connected manner.
Back to my example, all of us have many roles in life, and our consciousness is able to keep track of these more or less.
We remember that we're a teacher or a parent or a student or a spouse or a brother or a sister.
It's not like we forget these things.
But if we pay attention, we notice it's not always true.
These many roles and connections are more fluid than that.
Our version of the Heart Sutra opens right in the middle of a conversation, so it's a little bit confusing.
I talked about this at some length on Wednesday, so you can listen to that on the website later.
But I'll mention a few things just so we're on the same page.
Our sutra opens with the bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara, entering deeply into a practice.
It says, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, when deeply practicing Prajnaparamita, which is wisdom, a Buddhist gloss on wisdom, saw something.
It goes on a little bit about what she saw and what the effects of her vision were.
Then she starts talking, which isn't obvious the way our sutra is written out.
She starts talking to one of the Buddha's disciples, a character named Shariputra.
Before this, in a longer version of the sutra, the Buddha is there, as he is in all sutras.
And actually the Buddha doesn't say anything, which is a little bit strange.
Most of the sutras are the words of the Buddha directly, as remembered and written down by his students.
That's the mythology of it.
That's what a sutra is.
In this case, the Buddha is himself in a deep meditation when the sutra opens and describes where he is and who is there, as they always do.
Seemingly in response to the Buddha's deep meditation practice, Avalokiteshvara enters into this connection with wisdom, this wisdom meditation practice.
Then it says in there that the Buddha looks around the room.
Even though he's in meditation he can do lots of stuff, and he looks into people's minds.
He sees that one of his chief disciples, Shariputra, has a burning question.
Maybe, I don't know, Shariputra is aware of this question or not, but the Buddha can see that he has it.
Shariputra is famous in the early Buddhist writings as an expert on wisdom.
The idea is that Shariputra doesn't quite get what Avalokiteshvara is doing.
He can sense that Avalokiteshvara is in some kind of wisdom practice, but for all of his many practices and years of experience, he doesn't quite get it.
So the Buddha prompts Shariputra to ask Avalokiteshvara, what are you doing?
What's going on?
And he says something like, how should we practice deeply the wisdom, the wisdom beyond wisdom?
How should we do that?
Our sutra is actually completely Avalokiteshvara's answer to that question.
That's good to know, huh?
Who's this guy, Shariputra, and why is it going on like this?
Ours is the pithy, just-the-essential-thing version, so we can chant it quick and memorize it.
What Avalokiteshvara saw has to do with the nature of our experience as human beings and the nature of reality.
Somehow her clear understanding of this is incredibly beneficial.
It says in here, and most of us have chanted it many times, that she clearly saw that all five aggregates are empty, and thus relieved all suffering.
It's not just a little bit of suffering, not like she felt a little better or was having a good day.
It's more like complete freedom and ease in the middle of any kind of problem or joy.
Usually the way suffering is described, it's a little different from pain.
There can be pain and unpleasant sensations, but it doesn't mean you necessarily have to suffer.
So what are these five aggregates?
We talked about that a bunch on Wednesday.
Basically they're an early Buddhist psychological analysis, which in a Western frame wouldn't even be psychology, because the result of this psychology is that there's no psyche.
So it's psychology without a psyche.
But if you look carefully at what's happening, you see it's just different categories of experience.
The me, me, me, me, me that I was grappling with at 5 a.m. is just an artifact or a side effect of this series of experiences, and isn't as real as we think it is.

If we can see that our life is just a flow of independent, separate experiences, which are nevertheless interdependent, so they're individual and they're not at the same time, then we can really lighten up.
We don't have to worry about being a good person or a bad person or doing it right or doing it wrong, because we're just one factor amongst many.
We're still doing our best, of course, and having a good intention, but not feeling like the world's on our shoulders, because we are the world and the world is us.
Or all we are is a fluid series of experiences of worldness emerging through our own experience.
The sutra does a thorough job of telling us that this is the case, using Buddhist shorthand.
It says:
*Shariputra, form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself, form.*
Form is one of these categories: stuff.
The early Buddhists didn't think there was no stuff, or that it was at all an illusion.
They agreed with our common sense that there's some stuff here.
But they said, look twice.
Make sure you really know what the nature of this stuff is.
Maybe you're making some big assumptions based on language, based on not paying a lot of attention, based on being a little bit self-absorbed.
Maybe stuff has a little different nature than you think.
Emptiness is a description of its true nature in Mahayana Buddhist philosophy.
It's empty of solidity, empty of permanence, empty of separateness.
Pretty much anything we ascribe to it, maybe not quite that way.

The teaching that's connected to this, and helps it make sense, because this is a little bit hard to get: one of the great translators of this material from Sanskrit was a German-born scholar named Edward Conze.
He's kind of a funny guy.
He's no longer living.
I've told this story before, so I won't tell it now, but he's a fascinating guy.
As a scholar he never did meditation or anything like that, and there weren't as many options in the 30s and 40s when he was growing up in England.
He was a German-born guy living in England.
But somehow he was really caught by this teaching on emptiness and the way it's expressed in these Buddhist sutras.
What he said about emptiness in the Heart Sutra is this:
*This teaching is the true lion's roar, lion's roar from the great lion of the tribe of the Sakyas.*
That's the Buddhist tribe.
So the Buddha is the great lion of the tribe of the Sakyas, and this teaching is his roar.
*And those of you who have not fled out of earshot can now be told about it.
But we must think very hard and put a most unwelcome strain on our little gray cells if we want to appreciate the true implications of this teaching.*
Isn't that cute?
Your little gray cells.
Do you know Hercule Poirot?
He talks about his gray cells.
This is a harder mystery than Hercule Poirot could figure out, so it's a little bit baffling.
The connected teaching of dependent origination is really helpful because it makes a little more sense to us.
I've recently been reading a book by His Holiness the Dalai Lama about ethics, and he talks a bunch in it about dependent origination.
Basically the idea is that you really can't figure out how to behave in a graceful and sane way unless you have some sense of these teachings about reality.
That's why he brings this up, I guess.
But let's see what he says.
This is His Holiness:
*At a public talk I gave in Japan a few years ago, I saw some people coming towards me carrying a bunch of flowers.
I stood up in anticipation of receiving their offering.
But to my great surprise they walked straight past me and laid the flowers on the altar behind me.
I sat down feeling somewhat embarrassed.
And yet again I was reminded that the way in which things and events unfold does not coincide with our expectations.*
*Indeed, this fact of life, that there is often a gap between the way in which we perceive phenomena and the reality of any given situation, is a source of much unhappiness.
This is especially true, as in the example here, when we make judgments on the basis of a partial understanding, which turns out to not be fully justified.*
The real implication of these teachings on emptiness is that every understanding has this nature.
We're always not quite getting it.
And like Conze said, if you're not running out of the room, then you have a chance to learn something new here.
You can handle that idea that you don't get it and you never will.
Right?
Which is not what we wanted to hear when we grew up and were educated.
We wanted to get it.
The Dalai Lama goes on:
*When we consider these matters, we start to see that we cannot finally separate any one phenomena from its context.
Everything is determined by context.
We can only speak in terms of relationships.
In the course of our daily lives, we engage in countless different actions and receive huge amounts of sensory input from all that we encounter.

The problem of misperception, which of course does vary in degree, arises because of our tendency to isolate particular aspects of an event or experience and see those as constituting its totality, its reality.
And this leads to a narrowing of perspective, and from there to false expectations.*
So if we pick something out, we [unclear: "be shorthand"] for what's happening.
We do this.
You can watch your mind do this.
And then we backfill: okay, this is this kind of thing.
We're missing something.
*But when we consider reality itself, we quickly become aware of its infinite complexity.
We realize that our habitual perception of it is often inadequate.
If this were not so, this concept of deception would be meaningless.
If things and events always unfolded as we expected, there would be no illusion or misconception.*
The Tibetans are always thinking it forwards and backwards.
It's kind of great.
*As a means of understanding this complexity, I find the teaching of dependent origination as articulated by the Madhyamaka school of Buddhist philosophy to be particularly helpful.*
So here's one of the Mahayana schools.
*According to this, we can understand how things and events come to be in three different ways.
At the first level, we have the principle of cause and effect, whereby all things and events arise in dependence on a complex web of interrelated causes and conditions.*
So this makes sense, right?
Things arise according to a complex web of conditions.
But this is only one level.
He's saying one layer.
And this suggests that no thing or event can be construed as capable of coming into existence or remaining in existence all by itself.
For example, if I take some clay and mold it, I can bring a pot into being.

This pot exists as an effect of my actions, but at the same time it is also the effect of myriad other causes and conditions, including the combination of the clay and the water to form the raw material.
Beyond this, we can point to the coming together of molecules, atoms, and other minute particles which form its constituents.
And those themselves also depend on innumerable other factors.
Then there are the circumstances leading up to my decision to make the pot.
That's also a condition here, thought and intention.
These are the cooperative conditions of my actions as I give shape to this clay.
All these different factors make it clear that my pot cannot come into existence independent of its causes and conditions.
So it is dependently originated.
This teaching is called dependent origination: things originate dependent on other things.
So that's the first level, which makes sense.
We miss it anyway, but it's very simple, right?
On the second level, dependent origination can be understood in terms of the mutual dependence which exists between the parts and the whole.
Without parts, there can be no whole.
Without a whole, the concept of parts makes no sense.
The idea of a whole is predicated on parts.
But these parts themselves must be considered to be wholes comprised of their own parts.
So that's true, right?
We don't think about it.
But somehow we're sort of creating these categories of wholeness in what we perceive and think about.
On the third level, so that was the second level, parts and wholes are happening all the time.
On the third level, all phenomena can be understood to be dependently originated because when we analyze them we find that ultimately they lack independent identity.
This can be understood from the way in which we refer to certain phenomena.
For example, the words action and agent presuppose one another.
You can't have an action without an agent.
But then the other way is true too, which we don't think about.
We think an agent is a solid thing doing actions, but it goes both ways.
There's actually no agent unless there's actions.
Only because he or she has had children.
Otherwise a daughter or son is called that only in relationship to their having parents.
The same relationship of mutual dependence is seen in the language we use to describe everything, including trades or professions.
Individuals are called farmers on account of their work on the land.
Doctors are called doctors because of their work in medicine.
The one thing always creates another three different levels here.
This is down to the way we conceptualize reality.
As far as mental phenomena are concerned, this is not just stuff out there, it's in here too, we see that again there is dependence.
Here it lies between perceiver and perceived.
Take for example the perception of a flower.
First, in order for such a perception to arise, there must be a sense organ, the eye.
Second, there must be a condition, in this case the flower.
Third, in order for a perception to occur, there must be something which directs the focus of the perceiver to the object.
Somehow, you look at the flower.
Then, through the causal interaction of these several conditions, a cognitive event occurs that we call perception of a flower.
Let's look at that more carefully.
Is it only the operation of the sense faculty?
Or is it only the interaction between the faculty and the flower?
Is it something else?
We find, if we look very carefully, we cannot understand the concept of perception except in the context of an infinitely complex series of causes and conditions.
We could add language, we could add color, but we reduce all this down to: there's a flower over there.

So this psychology and philosophy is suggesting that there's a real benefit to paying more attention to how perception, categorization, language, and the creation of the world happens, because we do it habitually in a way that's narrow and causes separation.
Separation causes suffering.
So emptiness is saying that no individual thing has an inherent existence.
Independent origination is about how it all flows together.
One thing helps to apparently create another thing.
And we talked Wednesday night about the Heart Sutra and all the other Prajnaparamita Sutras, that there's a wonderful myth about them.

Because these particular teachings don't really show up in the early Buddhist teachings, in historical fact they were written later probably, but the great myth they came up with was that the Buddha himself did say these things, but people weren't ready.
They had to hide them until people would be ready.
So they hid them in the underwater palaces of the Nagas, or these sea serpents, or sentient sea serpents.
They have really cool palaces.
I don't know how they do it with underwater palaces, but they do.

But the thing I didn't tell you was there's a particular guy who somehow was able to go to the bottom of the ocean and pick this stuff up in the first century common era, I think, because he was first or second.
And his name was Nagarjuna.
He's one of the most important philosophers in Mahayana Buddhism.
He's the originator of this Madhyamaka school that the Dalai Lama mentioned.
And Nagarjuna did nothing but write on and on and on about emptiness and dependent origination.
You can see his whole thing, lots of different angles to it.
So I thought you might like to hear just a couple of verses amongst thousands.
This is from one of his most famous writings.
So Nagarjuna, who supposedly brought these teachings back to us, wrote,
*Whatever arises dependently is explained as empty.
Thus dependent attribution is the middle way.
Since there is nothing whatever that is not dependently existent, for this reason there is nothing whatsoever that is not empty.*
Got that?
Whatever arises dependently, which is like everything, is explained as empty.
Thus dependent attribution is the middle way.
Seeing things as interdependent.
*Since there is nothing whatever that is not dependently arisen, for that reason there is nothing whatever that is not empty.*
Many hundreds of years later, in Tibet, where is this?
Yeah, here we go.
A Tibetan teacher named Mipham came up with a neat way of looking at this.
He said,
*The nature of phenomena is like the reflection of the moon in the water.
Like the reflection itself.
That's the nature of reality of all phenomena.*
It's like a reflection.
When you're looking at the moon reflecting the water, it's the reflection.
And the appearance of the moon in the water is the expression of this process.
So this is interesting.
When we see a reflection of the moon in the water, we see an image, right?
We go through this rapid process with our senses and our [unclear: "conscience"].
We see an image of the moon.
We know that's not really the moon, right?
At least that's what we say.
We're here a little bit early.
What's really the moon, we say, is this other image that's over there, right up in the sky.
Is that really the moon?
That's another question.
What he's saying is, we can pay attention to the difference between the image and the reflection.
That these are actually two different things that we smoosh together.
Because we smoosh them together, we miss something about the process of how things come into existence.
So notice the process of perception and cognition and the appearance of things.
On the one hand, it's real enough.
You can see it, you know.
There's an image of the moon.
On the other hand, it's definitely not the moon.
And that's not the moon either, right?
That's also an image.
So where does this leave us?
A little bit baffled, maybe.
But that's okay.
That's on purpose.

The idea is that our certainty that we know the nature of reality and fix ourselves and others into a particular position and container and personality, style, whatever you want to call it, is the engine of suffering.
We see each other as reflections and moons as a co-originated expression of some bigger something that we call life.
Maybe we can soften up.
Maybe we can be much more flexible.
Maybe we can let go.
It's not too hard, in a way, to imagine an understanding of physical forms being empty.
Especially as we age, we see everything constantly changing, right?
All the world changing in form.
What was interesting about our sutra is it says not just form, but everything.
The other categories that are cognitive, internal categories of consciousness, are the same way.
Everything's empty.
Everything's coming into existence, passing away again.
No one thing is as solid or as independent as we think.
And this also applies to our desires, our thoughts, our emotions, what we perceive, whether it's a noisy trash truck we perceive, or the best meal of our life.
These are all empty.
And another way of talking about emptiness is these are also boundless.
Huge, vast, more subtle and complex than we could ever take in, right?
A lot of times the best meal of your life is because you actually paid attention to what it tasted like, right?
But still you couldn't taste it all.
Maybe every meal you have is the best meal of your life, but you didn't notice.

And this even applies to our very concept of who and what we are, and even to the nature of our own consciousness: that it's empty, it's boundless, it's dependently originated, it's coming and going, and it's co-created by everything in the universe.
So the freedom from suffering and fear, the Heart Sutra later mentions fear, the idea is that this arises from a deeply felt sense of this teaching, these teachings.
Understanding it intellectually, for sure, but that's like the image of the moon, right?
Also feeling it in our gut, breathing into it and out from it.
This Heart Sutra is trying to remind us that the way we fix ourselves and our universe is a little narrow.
It's a little bit of a disaster.
That we are much bigger than that.
Much more fluid than that.
That we're so big that we collapse back into empty space.
That we are infinitely flexible and resilient beyond any idea of something that can flex or something that can break.
So the Heart Sutra is really kind of like a call.
We hear in the distance, like, what was that?
A call in the distance to enter, to embrace our place in kind of like a cosmic world.
That is this world, and isn't at the same time.
So that's my talk two on the Heart Sutra.
Hopefully it wasn't too bad.

And the Heart Sutra goes on, which we won't really get into this time around, but we have in years past, to go through a longer and more elaborated list of all the elements of psychology, of Buddha psychology, and perception, elements of the Buddha's path, and say every one of them has this quality.
It's all empty.
And it uses the word no, it uses negation as a shorthand for emptiness.
So no eyes doesn't mean there aren't any eyes.
I think that's a famous story.
The young man who went on to be the legendary sixth ancestor in China, a guy named Huineng, supposedly he said as a boy you overheard the Heart Sutra.
And he said to some, I think he's an orphan, so he said to somebody, a guardian or a monk or something, I have eyes.
So that's true.
We're not saying that there's no eyes, that would be stupid.
But they aren't the eyes that we think they are.
And they aren't seeing what we think they're seeing.
So that's the idea of it all.
And it ends with the mantra.
So the mantra connects to our little ceremony today.
The idea is that the Buddha was born into this world as an expression of this mantra, of this teaching.
And the mantra, gate gate, para gate, parasam gate bodhisvaha, means like to really thoroughly do this practice.
Literally means gone, gone beyond, gone completely beyond, gone all the way completely beyond, yes, or wow, or wake up.
Actually bodhi means wake up.
It means wake up, yes.
Svaha is just an exclamation.
So thank you very much.
